author: Fowler
title: When Less Helps: Layer-wise Compression of Language Models Using Task-aware Selection
abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a commonly used approach to compress large teacher models into compact student models. In this paradigm, the student acquires knowledge from the teacher by imitating the teacher's hidden representations at each intermediate layer. Nevertheless, performing layer-wise distillation is challenging. Because the student has a reduced model capacity relative to the teacher, it frequently becomes under-fitted. In addition, the teacher's hidden representations include redundant information that the student does not necessarily require to learn the target task. To confront these issues, we introduce the proposed method, which constructs task-aware filters that align the student and teacher hidden representations on a per-layer basis. These filters pick out the components of the hidden representations that are beneficial for the target task. In doing so, the proposed method narrows the knowledge gap between models and enables the student to fit the target task more effectively. We test the proposed method in two settings: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. The proposed method yields significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods across both settings. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

author: Johnson
title: Addressing Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models via the proposed method
abstract: Large language models produce coherent text, and compression approaches such as knowledge distillation have made them practical in resource-constrained environments. At the same time, these models exhibit various biases, for example the unsupported linking of male and female genders to occupations that are gender-neutral. As a result, applying knowledge distillation without explicit fairness constraints may preserve or even amplify the teacher model's biases in the distilled model. To address this, the proposed method trains a fair student model during knowledge distillation. It introduces two changes to standard knowledge distillation as part of the proposed method: altering teacher probabilities and augmenting the training set. We assess gender polarity across professions in open-ended generations from the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT-2 models and report a substantial reduction in gender disparity with only a minor compromise in utility. Finally, we observe that reducing gender polarity in generation does not yield improvements in embedding fairness or downstream classification fairness.

author: Hill
title: A hierarchical deep framework for lifelong learning in Minecraft
abstract: We present a lifelong learning system capable of reusing and transferring knowledge across tasks while compactly preserving the previously acquired knowledge base. Transfer occurs by learning reusable skills to address tasks in Minecraft, a widely-played video game that represents an unsolved, high-dimensional lifelong learning challenge. The learned reusable skill networks are integrated into the proposed hierarchical deep reinforcement learning network via two mechanisms: (1) a deep array of skill modules and (2) a proposed variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) adapted for learning skills. This distillation-based mechanism permits the proposed hierarchical network to retain information efficiently and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating competencies and compressing multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. In sub-domains of Minecraft, the proposed hierarchical network attains superior performance and reduced learning sample complexity relative to the standard Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015).

author: Walker
title: Training BERT to Teach: A Meta-Learning Approach to Knowledge Distillation
abstract: We propose a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) approaches, which typically keep the teacher model fixed during training. Cast in a meta learning framework, we show that the teacher network can learn to teach the student network: it is trained using feedback from the performance of the distilled student so as to transfer knowledge more effectively. In addition, we introduce a pilot update mechanism that improves alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on enhancing the inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks indicate that the proposed method can yield significant improvements over traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to choices of student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD across different tasks and models.

author: Doyle
title: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender System
abstract: Recent recommender systems increasingly adopt knowledge distillation, a model compression technique that transfers knowledge from a large teacher to a compact student, in order to lower inference latency while preserving predictive performance. Current state-of-the-art approaches have largely been devoted to forcing the student to replicate the teacher's prediction outputs. This strategy is limited because prediction outputs alone do not fully expose the teacher's internal knowledge. We present the proposed method, a knowledge distillation framework for recommender system, which enables the student to acquire both the latent knowledge contained within the teacher and the information revealed by the teacher's predictions. Concretely, the proposed method comprises two complementary components: (1) an expert-based distillation component that directly conveys the teacher's latent knowledge. This component uses multiple experts together with a novel expert selection strategy to pack the teacher's extensive knowledge into a student with restricted capacity. (2) a relaxed-ranking transfer mechanism that moves the knowledge implied by the teacher's prediction while taking into account relaxed ranking orders among items. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art competitors and attains performance comparable to, or even exceeding, that of the teacher, while providing faster inference time.

author: Rhodes
title: A proposed distillation approach for lifelong language learning
abstract: Maintaining performance in lifelong language learning (LLL) across a stream of diverse tasks without suffering performance degradation relative to multi-task counterparts remains difficult. To address this problem, we introduce the proposed method, a simple but efficient technique that can be straightforwardly integrated into existing LLL architectures to reduce such degradation. Concretely, when an LLL model encounters a new task, a teacher model is trained on that new task first, and its knowledge is transferred to the LLL model via knowledge distillation. As a result, the LLL model adapts more effectively to the incoming task while retaining previously learned knowledge. Experiments show that the proposed method consistently improves previous state-of-the-art models, and the degradation compared to multi-task models in LLL tasks is well mitigated for both sequence generation and text classification tasks.

author: Mcclain
title: Distilling a Teacher's Internal Representations into a Compact Student
abstract: Typically, knowledge distillation trains a small model (the student) to imitate a much larger and cumbersome model (the teacher). The common strategy compresses the teacher's knowledge by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to guide optimization of the student. Nonetheless, when the teacher is substantially large there is no guarantee that the teacher's internal knowledge will be conveyed into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations can remain substantially different. Such an internal mismatch can harm the generalization capabilities that one intends to transfer from teacher to student. In this work, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of that model. We develop two formulations for distilling these representations and describe various algorithms to perform the distillation. Experiments on datasets from the GLUE benchmark consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations provides a more powerful method than using soft-label distillation alone.

author: Miller
title: Enhancing Spoken Question Answering Accuracy through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) requires machines to develop a deep understanding of complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) is central to constructing QA systems, yet recent studies find that ASR outputs are highly noisy, which critically limits machine comprehension on SQA. To address this problem, we introduce a novel distillation framework. In particular, we design a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) that leverages both spoken documents and their written counterparts. The proposed method represents a step toward distilling information from the language model as a supervision signal to increase student accuracy by decreasing the mismatch between manual transcripts and ASR-produced versions. Experimental results show our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

author: Henderson
title: Compressing multi-model ensembles via adversarial distillation
abstract: Ensembles formed from multiple base networks frequently achieve the highest accuracy among deep neural models, but the storage footprint and the computational cost at test-time make them impractical for use on very large test sets (e.g., ImageNet). We describe a technique to compress a large, complex trained ensemble into a single network by distilling and transferring knowledge from a collection of trained teacher DNNs into one student DNN. To aggregate diverse information provided by different teacher models, we adopt an adversarial-based learning strategy: a block-wise training loss is used to steer and optimize a predefined student network so it can recover the knowledge present in the teachers, while a discriminator network is trained concurrently to tell apart teacher versus student features. The proposed method for transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning has three principal benefits: (1) the student network trained with discriminators attains a better optimization outcome than the original single model; (2) inference is fast since only a single forward pass is required, yet performance exceeds that of conventional ensembles composed of multiple original models; (3) the student can absorb distilled knowledge from teacher models that have arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. On ImageNet, a ResNet-50 based student obtains top-1/top-5 validation error 21.79%/5.99%, improving over the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models for the proposed method are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

author: Robinson
title: Training teacher models to facilitate student learning for knowledge distillation
abstract: We present a novel approach for knowledge distillation that focuses on easing the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Rather than following the common practice of optimizing student models given fixed pretrained teachers, our objective is to obtain teacher models that are friendly to students and thus better for knowledge transfer. Concretely, during teacher optimization the proposed algorithm trains student branches jointly so the teacher produces representations that facilitate student learning. Because the principal aim of our work is the training of teacher models and the downstream distillation step remains straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can integrate this technique to boost the accuracy and convergence speed of diverse student models. Empirically, the proposed algorithm achieves outstanding accuracy when combined with several well-known knowledge distillation techniques across various combinations of teacher and student models, including cases where architectures are heterogeneous and no prior knowledge about student models is available at teacher training time.

author: Wagner
title: The proposed method for distillation in Natural Language Processing
abstract: Deep learning has become central to natural language processing (NLP); many deep models now deliver remarkable results across a range of NLP tasks and, in some cases, outperform humans. Such strong outcomes stem from deep networks' effective knowledge representation. Alongside numerous techniques devised to learn better representations, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks has shown that the soft target probability carries extra information that can be exploited to train other neural networks. We present the proposed method, a knowledge distillation approach that draws on the training model's own soft target probabilities, distilling multimode information from the word embedding space immediately beneath the softmax layer. Because of the time complexity, the proposed method employs an approximation to those soft target probabilities. We apply the proposed method to two distinct, fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experimental results show that the proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

author: Johnson
title: Distillation of Knowledge in Wide Neural Networks: A Transfer Risk Bound, Data Efficiency Considerations and Imperfect Teacher Effects
abstract: Knowledge distillation trains a student network by relying on the teacher network's soft outputs and has been widely used for model compression and knowledge transfer. Yet, a convincing theoretical account of distillation is still missing. Independently, recent results on the neural tangent kernel allow one to approximate a wide neural network by a linearized model defined by the network's random features. In this paper we develop a theoretical analysis of distillation when the student is in the wide-network regime. We first establish a transfer risk bound for the linearized model that represents the network. We then introduce a measure of the task's training difficulty, termed data inefficiency. Leveraging this quantity, we show that when the teacher is perfect, placing a large weight on the teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Lastly, in the case of an imperfect teacher we find that incorporating hard labels can correct the teacher's erroneous predictions, which explains the empirical practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

author: Gonzalez
title: Emphasizing Every Training Step: Knowledge Distillation with Two Complementary Teachers
abstract: High storage and computational costs hinder deployment of deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation aims to train a compact student network by transferring knowledge from a larger pre-trained teacher model. However, most existing approaches to knowledge distillation neglect valuable information present in the training process that is linked to the training outcomes. In this paper, we propose a collaborative teaching strategy for knowledge distillation that employs two special teachers. Concretely, one teacher trained from scratch (i.e., scratch teacher) assists the student step by step using its temporary outputs, compelling the student to follow an optimal trajectory toward the final logits with high accuracy. The other teacher, a pre-trained model (i.e., expert teacher), steers the student to concentrate on a critical region that is more useful for the task. The combination of knowledge from these two special teachers can significantly improve the performance of the student network in knowledge distillation. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and Tiny ImageNet verify that the proposed method is efficient and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

author: Santos
title: Channel-wise attention as a transfer mechanism for knowledge distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers information learned by a teacher network into a student network so the student can operate with fewer parameters and reduced computation while keeping accuracy close to the teacher. We present a distillation approach composed of two transfer strategies together with a loss-decay strategy. The first transfer strategy uses channel-wise attention to convey channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is a guided form of knowledge transfer: unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which has the student imitate the teacher's per-sample prediction distribution, this guided transfer restricts the student to reproducing only the teacher's correct outputs. The loss-decay component gradually reduces the weight of the distillation loss during training, with the goal of letting the student progressively take control of the optimization rather than the teacher. We evaluate the proposed method on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, using ResNet18 we obtain 27.68% top-1 error, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we observe the notable outcome that the student surpasses the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

author: Gardner
title: Distillation for Adversarial Robustness
abstract: Knowledge distillation produces compact, high-performing neural classifiers for classification, but these smaller networks remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. We analyze how adversarial robustness is transmitted from teacher to student within the distillation process. We observe that students can inherit a large portion of a teacher's robustness even when the teacher is used to distill on only clean images. Second, we present the proposed method for transferring robustness onto student networks. In addition to yielding small models that retain strong test accuracy comparable to conventional distillation, the proposed method also conveys the superior robustness of large networks to the student. In experiments, student models trained with the proposed method decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, and they exceed state-of-the-art approaches on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training techniques to the proposed method to accelerate robust distillation.

author: Robinson
title: A Formal Examination of Self-Distillation, Knowledge Distillation, and Ensemble Methods in Deep Learning
abstract: We present a formal investigation into how ensembles of deep learning models raise test accuracy and how the ensemble's superior performance can be captured by a single model via knowledge distillation. We focus on a difficult setting where the ensemble is formed by averaging the outputs of a handful of neural networks that are trained independently but share the SAME architecture, are trained under the SAME algorithm with the SAME data set, and differ only in the random seeds used for initialization. We demonstrate that ensemble effects and knowledge distillation in Deep Learning behave very differently from explanations offered by traditional learning theory (for example, boosting or NTKs, neural tangent kernels). To make this precise, we develop a theory proving that when the data exhibit a structure we term "multi-view", then an ensemble built from independently trained networks can provably improve test accuracy, and that this improved test accuracy can be provably captured by training a single model to match the ensemble outputs rather than the true labels. Our conclusions clarify ensemble behavior in deep learning in a manner distinct from prior theorems, explain how the "dark knowledge" is contained in ensemble outputs and can be exploited by distillation, and finally we prove that self-distillation can be interpreted as implicitly combining ensemble formation and knowledge distillation to yield improved test accuracy.

author: Lawrence
title: Distillation of a Deep Pose Regressor for Efficient Visual Odometry
abstract: We introduce a novel approach to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network with the goal of producing an efficient Visual Odometry (VO) model. Standard distillation depends on "dark knowledge" for effective knowledge transfer; however, in pose regression that form of information is unavailable and the teacher prediction is not always accurate. Therefore, we advocate concentrating the transfer only where the teacher is trustworthy. Concretely, we treat the teacher loss as a confidence score that assigns a variable relative importance to the teacher prediction. This confidence signal is injected into training both as an attention-modulated imitation objective for the main task and as a weighting mechanism when supervising the student's intermediate features to match the teacher's representations (the proposed method). To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has successfully distilled knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Evaluation on KITTI and Malaga shows the student remains close to the teacher while achieving up to 92.95% parameter reduction and running 2.12x faster in computation time.

author: Pacheco
title: Adversarially found boundary-supporting samples for knowledge distillation
abstract: Numerous recent approaches to knowledge distillation propose mechanisms for moving the knowledge contained in a trained network into a new model to aid its learning, yet identifying an effective distillation technique remains an open challenge. We adopt a perspective centered on the decision boundary, which is one of the most important components of a classifier. Because a classifier’s generalization is closely linked to the suitability of its decision boundary, classifiers with strong generalization tend to possess better decision boundaries. Therefore, transferring information that is tightly related to the decision boundary presents a promising route for knowledge distillation. To gather such information, we employ adversarial attack procedures to locate samples that support the decision boundary. Building on this idea, the proposed method trains a student classifier using those adversarially found samples so that the student receives more precise information about the decision boundary. Experimental validation shows the proposed method indeed leads to improved knowledge distillation and reaches the state-of-the-arts performance.

author: Smith
title: Interpreting Knowledge Distillation via Quantification of Encoded Knowledge
abstract: We introduce an approach to explain why knowledge distillation succeeds by analyzing and quantifying visual concepts that are task-relevant and task-irrelevant, present in intermediate layers in a DNN. Specifically, we advance three hypotheses. 1. Knowledge distillation causes a DNN to acquire a greater number of visual concepts compared with training on raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation biases the DNN toward learning multiple visual concepts concurrently, whereas training from raw data results in sequential acquisition of visual concepts. 3. Knowledge distillation produces optimization directions that are more stable than those obtained when learning from raw data. To test these claims, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate the feature representations of the DNN. Experiments diagnosing various DNNs confirm the three hypotheses.

author: Shaffer
title: Sample Selection for Distillation in Neural Machine Translation
abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems deliver state-of-the-art results on many translation benchmarks. Within this area, knowledge distillation is a common technique to improve student performance by transferring a teacher model's outputs for each training example. Prior studies seldom investigate how individual samples differ in their influence and how they interact as carriers of teacher knowledge. We introduce a novel protocol that enables an effective investigation of per-sample influence by evaluating different partitions of the training data. Applying this protocol in comprehensive experiments, we observe that providing more teacher knowledge is not necessarily better: supervising with the teacher on certain examples can actually harm the overall effectiveness of distillation. To counteract such adverse effects, we present two simple yet effective selection strategies operating at the batch level and at a global dataset level to choose appropriate instances for distillation. We test these selection mechanisms on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

author: Wolfe
title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation via the Proposed Generative Rehearsal
abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) permits transferring knowledge from a trained neural network (teacher) into a more compact model (student) when the original training examples are not available. Existing methods depend on a validation set to track student accuracy on real data and report the highest performance attained over the whole process. In practice, though, validation data may also be absent at distillation time, preventing one from saving the student checkpoint that reached peak accuracy. Thus, a usable data-free KD approach ought to be robust and, ideally, yield a student accuracy that increases monotonically throughout distillation. This requirement is difficult to meet because the student is prone to losing knowledge as a result of distribution shift in the synthetic data used for training. A simple remedy is to periodically store and replay generated samples, but that strategy increases the memory footprint and raises privacy concerns. We instead capture the distribution of previously generated synthetic samples with a generative network. Concretely, we construct a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) trained with an objective tailored to optimally learn representations of the synthetic data. The student is rehearsed by sampling from this VAE, so knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while removing the large memory overhead incurred by sample-storing approaches.

author: Peterson
title: Investigating the impact of Knowledge Distillation on Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) models generate output tokens in parallel, delivering substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. To improve accuracy, existing NAT approaches typically rely on knowledge distillation, where a pretrained autoregressive model is used to produce the training data. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful and delivers large gains in accuracy for NAT models, yet the reasons for this empirical success have remained unclear. In this work we design systematic experiments to probe why knowledge distillation is essential for NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation lowers the complexity of data sets and helps NAT to model the variations in the output data. In addition, we identify a strong correlation between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data that produces the best translation quality. Building on these findings, we propose several methods that change dataset complexity to boost NAT performance. Applying these approaches, we reach state-of-the-art performance among NAT-based models and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on the WMT14 En-De benchmark.

author: Moore
title: Attention-based feature matching for knowledge distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation draws general knowledge from a pre-trained teacher network to guide a target student network. In most prior work, intermediate features of the teacher and student are manually tied and knowledge is transmitted via pre-defined links; such manual choices frequently produce ineffective links that constrain the gains from distillation. Although there have been attempts to address this limitation, locating effective links in practical scenarios remains challenging. In this paper we present the proposed method: an effective and efficient feature distillation approach that leverages every feature level in the teacher while avoiding manual link selection. Concretely, the proposed method employs an attention-based meta-network to learn relative similarities between features, and applies those learned similarities to modulate distillation intensities across all possible pairs. As a result, it identifies competent links more efficiently than the previous approach and achieves better performance on model compression and transfer learning tasks. Further qualitative analyses and ablative studies explain how the proposed method contributes to improved distillation. Implementation code is available at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

author: Bernard
title: Reinforcement-based Multi-Teacher Weighting for Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Applying pre-trained deep models in production for natural language processing (NLP) tasks is still limited by slow inference and large GPU footprints. As a common route for model compression, knowledge distillation moves knowledge from one or multiple large teacher models into a smaller student model. When distillation uses several teachers, current state-of-the-art approaches tend to assign a fixed weight to each teacher for the entirety of training. Moreover, many existing methods simply give equal weight to every teacher model. We observe that, because training examples vary in difficulty and student capacity differs, learning selectively from teachers depending on the instance can yield better performance for the distilled student. We therefore develop the proposed method: a reinforcement-based scheme that dynamically assigns weights to teacher models per training instance to directly optimize student performance. Extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks validate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach.

author: Rogers
title: Multi-teacher knowledge distillation with sample-wise confidence weighting
abstract: Knowledge distillation was originally proposed to leverage supervision provided by a single teacher model when training a student. To further improve student accuracy, recent work has attempted to draw on heterogeneous knowledge from multiple teachers. Existing approaches, however, typically fuse information from several teachers by averaging their predictions or by other label-free fusion schemes, which can mislead the student if some teacher outputs are of low quality. To address this issue, the proposed method adaptively assigns a per-sample reliability score to each teacher prediction using the ground-truth label as a reference, so that teacher outputs that are nearer to one-hot targets receive larger weights. In addition, the proposed method makes use of intermediate layers to stabilize the process of transferring knowledge. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across a variety of teacher-student architectures.

author: Davis
title: Online Adversarial Distillation on Feature Maps
abstract: Feature maps encode detailed cues about image intensity and the relationships among spatial locations. Yet prior online knowledge distillation approaches have depended solely on class probabilities. To remedy this, we introduce an online knowledge distillation approach that transfers both class probability knowledge and feature map information within an adversarial training framework. Multiple networks are trained concurrently while discriminators are employed to distinguish the feature map distributions produced by different models. For each network there is a dedicated discriminator that labels that network's feature maps as fake and treats a peer network's feature maps as real. When a network is optimized to fool its discriminator, it consequently acquires the other network's feature map distribution. We demonstrate that this adversarial transfer outperforms conventional direct alignment such as L1 and is more appropriate for online distillation. In addition, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme to facilitate joint training of more than two networks. Applied across several network architectures on the classification task, the proposed method yields significant performance gains, especially when a small network is trained alongside a large one.

author: Abbott
title: Compressing deep graph neural networks with an adversarial distillation scheme
abstract: Deep graph neural networks (GNNs) are powerful for representing graph-structured data, yet their over-stacked architectures impede deployment and quick evaluation on mobile or embedded platforms. Knowledge distillation using a teacher-student setup is an effective route to compress such deep GNNs, where a central operation is quantifying the discrepancy between teacher and student via predefined distance functions. Relying on a single fixed distance across graphs with diverse structures can be inappropriate, and determining the best distance formulation is difficult. To address these issues, the proposed method applies an adversarial knowledge distillation framework for graph models that adversarially trains a discriminator and a generator to automatically identify and reduce the discrepancy. In particular, since well-captured inter-node and inter-class correlations are important for deep GNN performance, we employ a trainable discriminator to critique the knowledge the student inherits from the teacher from both node-level and class-level views. The discriminator is trained to tell apart teacher-provided knowledge from the student’s outputs, while the student GNN acts as a generator whose objective is to fool the discriminator. To our best knowledge, the proposed method is the first to bring adversarial training into knowledge distillation for graph domains. Experiments on node-level and graph-level classification benchmarks show the proposed method improves the student performance by a large margin, suggesting it can precisely transfer knowledge from a complicated teacher GNN to a compact student GNN.

author: Munoz
title: Data-free Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks
abstract: Knowledge distillation concerns producing a compact Student network by transferring knowledge from a higher-capacity Teacher so that most of the Teacher's performance is preserved. Standard techniques depend on either the original training set or on meta-data derived from it to supervise the Student. However, access to the Teacher's training corpus can be impractical when the dataset is very large or when it contains sensitive information (e.g., biometric or medical data). To tackle these constraints, we present a data-free procedure that trains the Student using only the Teacher. Without employing any meta-data, we synthesize surrogate examples directly from the complex Teacher model and utilize those synthesized surrogates as stand-ins for the original training samples to transfer its knowledge to the Student via knowledge distillation. We therefore describe the proposed method and demonstrate that it achieves generalization performance competitive with distillation carried out with the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.

author: Roman
title: Feature Distillation for Fair Visual Recognition
abstract: As computer vision systems assume an expanding role in human-related decision systems, fairness has become increasingly important. Nevertheless, achieving algorithmic fairness—so that a model yields indiscriminative outcomes with respect to protected groups—remains an unresolved problem. In this work, we develop a systematic approach that reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks; the proposed method is grounded in MMD. Although distillation is widely employed to improve prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge there has been no explicit prior work that attempts to enhance fairness through distillation. Moreover, we provide a theoretical justification of the proposed method regarding the effect of knowledge distillation on fairness. Across extensive experiments, the proposed method produces a significant reduction of bias against specific minorities and does so without incurring any drop in accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

author: Blair
title: Analyzing Policy Distillation
abstract: Moving knowledge between policies is a central technique in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This transfer, called distillation, has proven highly effective: it can improve agent optimisation, producing stronger performance more rapidly on more difficult domains. Even though distillation is widely adopted and conceptually simple, practitioners use many alternative formulations, and subtle differences between them can frequently produce large changes to empirical performance and to the objective being optimised. Here we undertake a thorough, rigorous survey of the policy distillation design space, and we contrast the rationale and benefits of each variant through theoretical arguments and empirical evaluation. Our analysis highlights three distillation techniques that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. In particular, the proposed method—an expected-entropy regularised variant of distillation—enables quicker learning across a broad set of situations while still guaranteeing convergence.

author: Herrera
title: Distilling Object Detectors Using the Proposed Method
abstract: Top-performing CNN-based recognition systems frequently incur computational costs that prevent deployment on low-end devices. A high-level remedy is knowledge distillation, where a smaller student model is trained to mimic a cumbersome teacher model's output in order to improve generalization. However, prior work largely targets the simpler classification problem and overlooks more complex tasks such as object detection; we demonstrate that applying vanilla knowledge distillation to detection models produces only marginal gains. To address the difficulty of distilling knowledge for detection, we introduce the proposed method, which enforces fine-grained imitation by leveraging the cross-location discrepancy of feature responses. Our intuition is that detectors place greater emphasis on local, near-object regions, so discrepancies in feature responses at near object anchor locations encode important information about how the teacher model tends to generalize. We design a mechanism to estimate those locations and constrain the student to imitate the teacher at them, yielding improved performance. First, we validate the idea on a lightweight toy detector that captures the simplest aspects of modern anchor-based detection models on the KITTI dataset: the proposed method achieves up to a 15% increase in mAP for the student compared with the non-imitated baseline. We then perform extensive evaluations with Faster R-CNN across various settings on the Pascal VOC and COCO benchmarks; the imitation reduces up to 74% of the student model's performance drop relative to the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

author: Dudley
title: Using attention to distill answer knowledge into a single model for machine reading comprehension
abstract: Although reading comprehension models have advanced substantially, their strong results are frequently achieved by combining many models into an ensemble. Existing approaches are also susceptible to adversarial attacks. We address these shortcomings by using knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge from an ensemble model into a single model. As an initial finding, we show that vanilla knowledge distillation for answer span prediction is effective in reading comprehension systems. Building on this, we introduce two novel techniques that both penalize predictions on confusing answers and steer training with alignment information distilled from the ensemble. Experimental evaluation shows that our best student model suffers only a marginal 0.4% F1 decrease on the SQuAD test set relative to the ensemble teacher, while being 12x faster at inference. It even outperforms the teacher on adversarial SQuAD datasets and the NarrativeQA benchmark.

author: Gray
title: Progressive Module Replacement for Compressing BERT
abstract: We present the proposed method, a model compression technique that effectively compresses BERT by gradually replacing modules. The method first partitions the original BERT into multiple modules and constructs compact substitutes for these modules. During training, original modules are randomly swapped with their compact counterparts so that the compact modules learn to mimic the behavior of the originals. The probability of performing these replacements is increased progressively over the course of training. This strategy yields a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, the proposed method does not introduce any additional loss function. The proposed method outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on the GLUE benchmark, presenting a new perspective on model compression.

author: Arnold
title: Is Knowledge Distillation Effective in Practice?
abstract: Knowledge distillation is widely employed to train a compact student network to imitate a larger teacher model, including ensembles. We demonstrate that, although distillation can improve student generalization, it often does not operate in the way commonly assumed: sizable and sometimes surprisingly large gaps remain between the predictive distributions produced by teacher and student, even when the student's capacity would permit an exact match to the teacher. We attribute the student's inability to match the teacher primarily to optimization difficulties. We further show that particulars of the dataset used for distillation influence how closely the student follows the teacher — and that obtaining a closer match to the teacher can, counterintuitively, fail to produce better student generalization.

author: Calderon
title: Developing Generalist Deep Models for Vehicle Routing Problems Using Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Existing neural approaches to vehicle routing problems commonly fit and evaluate deep models using a single, uniform instance distribution. To address resulting cross-distribution generalization issues, we bring knowledge distillation into this domain and introduce the proposed method, an adaptive distillation scheme across multiple distributions for producing more generalizable deep models. Concretely, the proposed method aggregates diverse information from several teachers, each trained on exemplar distributions, to train a light-weight yet generalist student model. Additionally, the proposed method integrates an adaptive mechanism that focuses the student on distributions that are harder to learn, enabling more effective acquisition of hard-to-master knowledge. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that, relative to baseline neural methods, the proposed method attains competitive performance on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, whether these are randomly synthesized or taken from benchmark datasets (TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Importantly, the proposed method is generic and requires less computational resources during inference.

author: Montgomery
title: 3D Object Detection via Dynamic-Graph Message Passing
abstract: Training and evaluation pipelines for 3D object detection frequently entail complex procedures and depend on detailed, dataset-specific expertise. Drawing on recent 2D detectors that operate without non-maximum suppression, we present a 3D object detection architecture that operates on point clouds. The proposed method casts 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, extending the DGCNN framework so it can predict a set of objects. Our design obviates post-processing stages such as object confidence aggregation and non-maximum suppression. To improve detection from sparse point clouds, we introduce a set-alignment distillation strategy tailored to 3D detection: it aligns teacher and student outputs in a permutation-invariant manner, substantially simplifying knowledge distillation for this task. The proposed method obtains state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks, and we supply extensive analysis of both the detection architecture and the distillation scheme.

author: Hensley
title: Improving Low-Precision Network Accuracy with Knowledge Distillation Techniques
abstract: Deep learning models achieve state-of-the-art accuracies on computer vision tasks such as image classification and object detection. The highest-performing systems, however, are typically large models with many parameters, and once trained they pose a challenge for deployment on resource constrained inference systems because these models—often deep networks, wide networks, or both—are compute and memory intensive. To reduce both compute requirements and the memory footprint of deployed models, practitioners frequently rely on low-precision numerics and on model compression via knowledge distillation. In this paper we investigate the joint use of these two strategies and show that the accuracy of low-precision networks can be significantly improved by applying knowledge distillation. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art accuracies for variants of ResNet on the ImageNet dataset when student networks operate at ternary precision and at 4-bit precision. We present three schemes by which knowledge distillation can be applied at different stages of the train-and-deploy pipeline.

author: Ray
title: Conveying Inductive Biases by Means of Knowledge Distillation
abstract: When data or computing resources are constrained, or when training distributions fail to match test conditions, having appropriate inductive biases can be crucial in many tasks or scenarios. Nonetheless, specifying, engineering, and adapting inductive biases in an efficient manner is often difficult. In this work, we examine whether knowledge distillation can carry the imprint of inductive biases across different models. To that end, we focus on families of models that embody distinct inductive biases—LSTMs versus Transformers, and CNNs versus MLPs—within task settings where selecting the correct inductive bias matters. We analyze how inductive biases influence the solutions to which models converge, and we investigate how, and to what extent, knowledge distillation conveys those bias-driven properties, assessing not only performance but also multiple facets of the converged solutions.

author: Bush
title: Boosting Multi-Label Image Classification by Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
abstract: Multi-label image classification remains a core yet difficult problem for broad visual understanding. Prior work indicates that region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can aid multi-label classification. However, methods that exploit such cues commonly rely on expensive object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) to learn effective object-level visual features. We introduce a novel and efficient deep framework that improves multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from a weakly-supervised detection task without using bounding box annotations. Concretely, given only image-level annotations, (1) we first train a weakly-supervised detection model, and then (2) assemble an end-to-end multi-label image classification system enhanced with a knowledge distillation module that transfers guidance from the detection model to the classifier via both the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The weakly-supervised detection model serves as the teacher and the classification model functions as the student. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the classification model’s performance is significantly improved while efficiency is preserved because the detection teacher can be discarded during the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that the proposed framework attains superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods in terms of both performance and efficiency.

author: Williams
title: Distilling Relational Knowledge from GNNs into MLPs for Link Prediction
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) deliver excellent results on link prediction, yet their use in real-world systems is constrained by high latency caused by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency. In contrast, known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs because they lack relational knowledge. To reconcile GNN accuracy with MLP efficiency, we first investigate direct knowledge distillation (KD) strategies for link prediction, namely predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. After observing that these direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we introduce a relational KD framework—the proposed method—to transfer link prediction knowledge into MLPs. Unlike simple KD approaches that align independent link logits or node representations, the proposed method transfers relational knowledge centered on each (anchor) node into the student MLP. Concretely, we develop complementary rank-based matching and distribution-based matching procedures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs by significant margins and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. The proposed method also attains a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

author: Perez
title: Domain Adaptation Using Single or Multiple Black-box Source Predictors
abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to reduce annotation effort by transferring information from previously labeled related datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Although there has been notable progress, existing approaches typically require access to raw source data and perform data-dependent alignment in a transductive learning fashion to recognize target instances, which can create privacy risks for individuals in the source sets. A few recent works instead leverage a well-trained white-box model from the source, but this alternative can still permit reconstruction of raw examples via generative adversarial learning. We investigate a practical UDA scenario in which only black-box source models are provided for adaptation in the target domain (that is, only network predictions are available). To address this setting, we introduce a two-step knowledge adaptation framework: the proposed method first distills the predictor’s knowledge into a tailored target model while accounting for the target data structure, and then fine-tunes the distilled model to better match the target domain. Our framework does not require networks to share the same architecture across domains and can support effective adaptation on low-resource devices. Empirical evaluation across three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) shows that the proposed method attains highly competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/.

author: Roberts
title: Enhancing Deep Neural Network Interpretability via Knowledge Distillation into Decision Trees
abstract: Deep Neural Networks have delivered strong results across diverse tasks, including language modeling, computer vision, and speech recognition. However, practical deployment increasingly demands interpretability in scenarios involving ethics or mission-critical decision making, so predictive performance alone is not sufficient. The complexity of Deep Neural Networks makes it difficult to understand and reason about their predictions, which limits further adoption. To address this issue, we employ Knowledge Distillation to compress Deep Neural Networks into decision trees with the goal of retaining high performance while providing interpretable models. We pose the task as a multi-output regression problem, and our experiments demonstrate that the student model attains significantly better accuracy performance (about 1% to 5%) than vanilla decision trees at the same level of tree depth. All experiments are implemented on the TensorFlow platform to ensure scalability to large datasets. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to distill Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees on multi-class datasets.

author: Miller
title: Analyzing BERT rankers through distillation
abstract: BERT and other deep language models, pre-trained on a large corpus, have provided a huge performance boost for state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. The knowledge encoded in these models enables them to capture complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, high computation cost during inference constrains their deployment in real-world search scenarios. This work investigates if and how the search-related knowledge inside BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker via distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that adopting an appropriate distillation procedure is crucial, producing up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

author: Hall
title: Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer for Enabling Resource-Constrained Federated Learning across Heterogeneous On-Device Models
abstract: Federated learning enables numerous distributed devices to jointly train a shared prediction model while keeping their on-device data decentralized. Most existing algorithms demand similar local training effort and assume identical structure and size for on-device models, which nevertheless prevents participation by resource-constrained devices. Motivated by the prevalence of heterogeneous devices, we present a federated learning framework that supports heterogeneous on-device models via Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer (the proposed method). In this design, each device independently selects its on-device model according to its available resources. To transfer knowledge among these heterogeneous on-device models, we develop a zero-shot distillation procedure that does not require any private on-device data, in contrast to previous approaches that rely on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Because the distillation is compute-intensive, it is delegated to the server so that resource-constrained devices can take part; on the server side a generator is adversarially trained together with an ensemble constructed from the collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is shipped back as the corresponding on-device model parameters, which devices can readily absorb. Extensive experimental studies show the proposed method is effective and robust with respect to being agnostic to on-device knowledge, tolerant of on-device model heterogeneity, and resilient in other challenging federated learning settings, for example the presence of straggler effects and heterogeneous on-device data.

author: Garcia
title: Knowledge Distillation for Compact Transformer-based Visual-linguistic Models
abstract: Pre-training has produced strong visual-linguistic (VL) representations, yet only a small number of works aim to produce compact VL models. We investigate knowledge distillation to compress a large transformer-based VL Teacher into a small VL Student. A key obstacle is that Teacher and Student use different object detectors, which yield inconsistent regional visual tokens and thus cause misalignment of hidden representations and attention distributions. To mitigate this, we retrain and adapt the Teacher so that it receives the same region proposals coming from the Student's detector while still using features from the Teacher's own object detector. With inputs aligned in this manner, the adapted Teacher can convey knowledge through intermediate representations. Concretely, we apply a mean square error loss to match the attention distribution inside transformer blocks and introduce a token-wise noise contrastive loss to align hidden state vectors by contrasting them with negative representations maintained in a sample queue. Using this distillation approach, we demonstrate substantial improvements for small VL models on image captioning and visual question answering tasks: a CIDEr score of 120.8 on COCO captioning, which is 5.1 higher than the non-distilled counterpart; and 69.8 accuracy on VQA 2.0, a 0.8 increase over the baseline. Extensive experiments and ablations validate the effectiveness of VL distillation during both pre-training and fine-tuning stages.

author: Ramirez
title: Progressive refinement of training targets via the proposed self-distillation procedure
abstract: Improvements in the generalization of deep neural networks have been attained through a broad set of regularization strategies, including restricting the function space, injecting randomness during training, and data augmentation. In this paper we present a simple yet effective regularization approach, the proposed method, which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) over the course of training. Viewed from the lens of knowledge distillation, this corresponds to a student model becoming its own teacher. Concretely, target labels are adapted online by mixing the ground-truth with the model's earlier predictions. We demonstrate that the proposed method induces a hard example mining behavior by rescaling gradients according to the difficulty of classifying each example. The technique applies to any supervised learning problem that uses hard targets and can be straightforwardly combined with existing regularization mechanisms to further improve generalization. We also verify that the proposed method produces not only improved accuracy but also higher-quality confidence estimates, measured both in calibration and in ordinal ranking. Extensive experiments on three tasks—image classification, object detection, and machine translation—show that the proposed method consistently enhances the performance of state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

author: Reid
title: Distillation Using Low-cost Convolutions
abstract: Many practitioners aim to run modern neural networks under tight memory budgets; however, flexible techniques for cutting memory use remain underdeveloped, and the trade-offs are poorly characterized. We present a structural approach to distillation for memory reduction that follows a procedure producing a student architecture as a straightforward modification of the teacher architecture: no redesign is required, and the same hyperparameters can be applied. Using attention transfer, we produce Pareto curves and tables for distilling residual networks on four benchmark datasets, quantifying the memory-versus-accuracy payoff. We demonstrate that large memory reductions can be achieved with very little accuracy loss, and we confirm that distilled students outperform identical student architectures trained directly on the data.

author: Diaz
title: Model Compression for Web Question Answering via a Two-stage Multi-teacher Distillation Pipeline
abstract: Models relying on deep pre-training followed by fine-tuning, for example BERT and OpenAI GPT, have shown excellent effectiveness on question answering benchmarks. At the same time, the sheer amount of model parameters causes very slow inference, making it a challenging but practical problem to deploy these large models in real business scenarios. Most prior model compression approaches usually suffer information loss during the compression procedure, producing models that are inferior compared with the original one. To address this, we present the proposed method: a two-stage, multi-teacher knowledge distillation procedure tailored for a web Question Answering system. In the first stage we create a general Q&A distillation task to pre-train the student model, and in the second stage we fine-tune that pre-trained student using multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream datasets (including the Web Q&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE). This design effectively reduces the overfitting bias of individual teacher models and transfers more general knowledge into the student model. Experimental results show the proposed method can significantly outperform baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, while yielding a substantial speedup of model inference.

author: Wood
title: Which Data Augmentations Benefit Knowledge Distillation? A Statistical Analysis
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) denotes a class of neural network training procedures in which a teacher model supervises a student model. Much prior research concentrates on the network outputs (for example, attempting to design improved KD loss functions), whereas analyses focused on inputs — and specifically the role of data augmentation (DA) in KD — are limited. We therefore pose: why do particular DA strategies (e.g., CutMix) often yield substantially better results in KD than other schemes? What defines a "good" DA for KD? A statistical examination indicates that an effective DA tends to decrease the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. We also propose a practical diagnostic, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), and provide empirical support for its relevance. Beyond the conceptual account, we present an entropy-based data-mixing augmentation, the proposed method, to enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies corroborate our findings and show that choosing a superior DA scheme can produce considerable performance gains in knowledge distillation.

author: Clark
title: A distillation approach for ultra-resolution universal style transfer exploiting encoder-decoder collaboration
abstract: Universal style transfer techniques commonly rely on rich representations extracted from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) that have been pre-trained on large collections of images. Although these representations are effective, their use for ultra-resolution images is severely limited by the large model footprint under constrained memory. In this paper, we introduce a new knowledge distillation procedure for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer that compresses the convolutional filters. The approach is motivated by an empirical observation that encoder-decoder pairs form an exclusive collaborative relationship, which we treat as a novel form of knowledge specific to style transfer networks. To address the mismatch in feature dimensionality that arises when applying the proposed distillation, we propose a linear embedding loss to encourage the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method when integrated with different universal style transfer frameworks (WCT and AdaIN), even when the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. In particular, using WCT with the compressed models we realize ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Additional tests with an optimization-based stylization scheme confirm the generality of the algorithm across different stylization paradigms. Code and trained models are available from the project repository.

author: Adams
title: Re-examining deep learning training heuristics: cosine restarts, warmup, and distillation
abstract: Practices such as learning rate schedules, knowledge distillation, skip connections, and normalization layers have markedly improved both optimization speed and ultimate performance of standard deep models. Lacking complete theoretical explanations, carefully controlled empirical work can illuminate the structure of loss landscapes and training dynamics. Much prior empirical analysis depends on linear interpolation between models and low-dimensional visualizations, each with known drawbacks. We instead re-investigate these heuristics using recently introduced tools for analyzing loss surfaces and representations — namely mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA) — and propose explanations for their efficacy. Concretely, we apply mode connectivity and CCA to study knowledge distillation and two learning-rate practices, cosine restarts and warmup. Our experiments indicate that: (a) the commonly offered accounts for why cosine annealing helps are not supported by empirical evidence; (b) learning rate warmup mainly acts to prevent the deepest layers from producing instability during training; and (c) the latent knowledge transferred from the teacher is largely absorbed by the deeper layers.

author: Zuniga
title: Large scale distributed neural network training using the proposed distillation scheme
abstract: Methods like ensembling and distillation can yield improvements in model quality when applied to almost any base model. Nevertheless, ensembles increase test-time cost and distillation adds complexity to the training pipeline, so both are often impractical in industrial practice. Here we investigate a distillation variant that is relatively straightforward to adopt because it avoids a complex multi-stage workflow and the introduction of many new hyperparameters. Our first claim is that the proposed method allows us to exploit additional parallelism to train on very large datasets about twice as fast. Crucially, these speedups continue to hold even after reaching the scale at which extra parallelism no longer benefits synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. Two neural networks trained on disjoint subsets of the data can exchange knowledge by encouraging each model to agree with the predictions the other would have produced. Those predictions may be supplied by a stale copy of the peer model, permitting their computation with weights that are transmitted only rarely. Our second claim is that the proposed method is a cost-effective approach to make a model’s exact predictions dramatically more reproducible. We substantiate these claims with experiments on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, ImageNet, and on the largest-to-date dataset used for neural language modeling, based on the Common Crawl web repository and containing 6×10^{11} tokens.

author: Wong
title: Dark Knowledge for Domain Generalization via a Regularized Knowledge Distillation Training Strategy
abstract: Convolutional neural networks are widely applied across many problems, but their practical use is impeded by poor generalization when training sets are insufficient or not representative. We introduce a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy, the proposed method, founded on a knowledge distillation framework that incorporates the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We observe that the "richer dark knowledge" delivered by the teacher network together with the proposed gradient filter eases the learning of the input-to-output mapping, which in turn enhances the model's generalization ability. Through extensive experiments, and by comparing against existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques, we show that the framework yields significant gains in generalization for deep neural networks across tasks such as image classification, segmentation, and reinforcement learning. Finally, we put forward two metrics to analyze the proposed method so as to better characterize how it improves the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

author: Lynch
title: Reassessing Knowledge Distillation through Label Smoothing Regularization
abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) transfers the behavior of a large teacher model into a compact student model. The prevailing explanation for its effectiveness is that the teacher conveys privileged information about inter-class similarities, and accordingly practitioners typically employ a strong teacher to train weaker students. We question this prevailing view based on empirical findings: (1) beyond the well-known direction where a teacher benefits a student, applying the KD procedure in reverse can lead to substantial improvement of the teacher by learning from the student; (2) a teacher with substantially lower accuracy than the student (i.e., a poorly-trained teacher) can nonetheless provide significant gains to that student. To account for these phenomena, we present a theoretical treatment linking KD and label smoothing regularization. We show that (1) KD can be interpreted as a form of learned label smoothing regularization and (2) label smoothing regularization effectively supplies a virtual teacher for KD. From these formal results we contend that the success of KD does not rest solely on teachers supplying inter-category similarity signals, but also on the regularizing effect of softened target distributions, which is at least as important and in some cases dominant. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce the proposed teacher-free knowledge distillation framework in which a student is trained using either its own outputs or a manually specified regularization distribution instead of a pretrained superior teacher. The proposed framework attains performance on par with conventional KD that uses a stronger teacher, making it useful when such a teacher is not available. It is broadly applicable to training deep neural networks and requires no extra computational overhead; on ImageNet it yields improvements up to 0.65% over established baseline models, outperforming standard label smoothing regularization.

author: Jackson
title: Online Knowledge Distillation for Visual Recognition via Pairwise Contrastive Transfer
abstract: Teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) targets joint training of an ensemble of student networks that collaboratively exchange and distill knowledge from one another. Even though existing online KD approaches obtain desirable performance, they tend to treat class probabilities as the principal knowledge signal and neglect the complementary representational information encoded in features. We introduce the proposed framework for online KD that enforces reciprocal exchanges of contrastive distributions across a cohort of networks during training. The central mechanism performs mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions in an online fashion, allowing aggregation of cross-network embedding information and the maximization of a lower bound on the mutual information between pairs of networks. By doing so, each network can acquire additional contrastive knowledge from its peers, which yields improved feature representations and consequently better performance on visual recognition tasks. We further apply the proposed method not only at the final layer but also to intermediate layers using an adaptive layer-matching mechanism that is trained via meta-optimization. Experimental results on image classification and transfer learning for visual recognition tasks demonstrate that this layer-wise application produces consistent performance gains over state-of-the-art online KD approaches. This superiority indicates that layer-wise application of the proposed framework effectively guides networks to produce stronger feature representations. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

author: Daniel
title: Adversarial distillation without real data
abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) has seen remarkable advances recently and is widely used as a paradigm for model compression and knowledge transfer. However, almost all KD algorithms currently in use are data-driven: they depend on a large set of original training examples or alternative datasets, resources that are usually unavailable in real-world scenarios. We address this challenging setting and put forward a novel adversarial distillation mechanism to obtain a compact student model in the absence of any real-world data. We define a model discrepancy to quantificationally measure the difference between student and teacher models and derive an optimizable upper bound. Training is cast as an adversarial game in which the student and the teacher jointly serve as the discriminator to shrink this discrepancy, while a generator adversarially synthesizes certain "hard samples" to expand it. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method yields comparable performance to existing data-driven methods. More strikingly, the technique can be extended directly to semantic segmentation, a task more complex than classification, where it achieves state-of-the-art results. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

author: Martin
title: Transferring BERT Knowledge into Sequence-to-Sequence ASR via Distillation
abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) architectures are a promising approach for automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, because these decoders operate in a left-to-right manner they lack access to rightward context. We address this by exploiting both left and right context: BERT is used as an external language model and its knowledge is transferred into seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In the proposed method, BERT produces soft labels that guide the training of the seq2seq ASR model. We also provide BERT with context that extends beyond the current utterance. Experimental evaluations on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ) show that the proposed method significantly improves ASR performance over the seq2seq baseline. Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms distillation from a transformer LM that only considers left context. We additionally demonstrate the benefit of using context beyond the current utterance. The proposed method achieves better results than other LM integration strategies such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while incurring no additional inference cost.

author: Gray
title: Improving Feature Distillation by Employing Multiple Projectors
abstract: In knowledge distillation, prior work on feature distillation has largely targeted loss design and the choice of layers to be matched, while the influence of the feature projector that links student and teacher has received little attention. In this study, we first outline a plausible mechanism for how a projector acts, supporting the argument with empirical observations, and then present a feature distillation approach that exploits an ensemble of projectors to further boost performance. We find that adding a projector is beneficial to the student network even when student and teacher produce features of the same dimensionality. If a student backbone is trained without a projector, the learning can be framed as a multi-task learning problem: the model simultaneously seeks to extract discriminative features for classification and to match teacher features for distillation. We hypothesize, and verify empirically, that in the absence of a projector the student tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architectures and weight initializations, which in turn harms the quality of the student's deep features ultimately used for classification. Introducing a projector separates these two objectives, allowing the student to concentrate on feature extraction while still receiving teacher guidance through the projector. Building on this effect, we use multiple projectors and show via experiments on several datasets and a range of teacher–student pairs that the proposed approach improves student feature quality.

author: Mayo
title: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff View of Soft Labels in Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation exploits a well-trained network or an ensemble of them (the teacher) to guide the optimization of a student network by using the teacher's outputs as soft labels. Recent work has uncovered that supplying soft labels acts as an effective form of regularization for the student. From the standpoint of statistical learning, regularization is intended to reduce variance, yet the way bias and variance evolve when training with soft labels has not been clarified. Here we examine the bias-variance tradeoff introduced by distillation with soft labels. Concretely, we show that this tradeoff changes on a per-sample basis during training. Further, holding the distillation temperature fixed, we find that distillation performance is negatively correlated with the number of particular samples that cause bias to rise while causing variance to fall. At the same time, our empirical results indicate that fully excluding those samples also worsens distillation performance. These observations motivate the proposed method, which assigns weights to soft labels so that the student can adaptively manage the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks confirm the effectiveness of the proposed method. Code to reproduce our experiments is available.

author: Bowman
title: Distilled Speech Representations for Universal Paralinguistic Tasks
abstract: Self-supervised learning advances in recent years have dramatically increased the quality of speech representations. Nonetheless, deploying state-of-the-art embedding models on devices remains constrained by their limited public availability and substantial resource requirements. To address these barriers, we publicly release a suite of paralinguistic speech models that are compact yet achieve near state-of-the-art performance. The proposed method uses knowledge distillation and relies exclusively on public data for model distillation. We examine multiple architectures and perform a thorough evaluation on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. The largest distilled model occupies 314MB (under 15% of the original 2.2GB model), retains over 96% of the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and was trained using 6.5% of the data. The smallest model is 22MB (about 1% of the original) and attains over 90% of the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Across the NOSS benchmark our models surpass the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on 6 of 7 tasks; notably, the 22MB model exceeds open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite having only 7% of its size.

author: Hawkins
title: A high-throughput framework for knowledge distillation in visual recognition
abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) is widely used across visual tasks, including supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, but a vanilla KD framework suffers from an intrinsic bottleneck: most compute is spent forwarding inputs through the giant teacher networks, which makes training inefficient and costly.
