A recent solution proposes building a label map over the whole image and, during training, obtains cropped region-level supervision by RoI aligning against this precomputed map; this avoids repeatedly querying the teachers and so reduces supervision overhead. Because those KD teachers were trained with conventional multi-crop protocols, however, inconsistencies arise between the global label-map and the region-level label produced by that scheme, which degrades performance. In this work we introduce the proposed framework that reproduces the distillation training behavior to synthesize soft labels using the multi-crop KD strategy, while operating faster than the recent solution since it removes post-processing steps such as RoI align and softmax operations. When multi-crop patches are loaded from the same image at data-loading time, the proposed framework attains greater efficiency than a standard image classification pipeline. On ImageNet-1K we achieve 79.8% with ResNet-50, improving by ~1.0% over the prior approach while also running faster. We further demonstrate an efficiency benefit on a self-supervised learning task. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

author: Cohen
title: Attention-guided fusion of teacher layers for knowledge distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation is used as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, a teacher and a student, are trained together. The teacher is treated as a trustworthy predictor and the student attempts to imitate its outputs. Typically a student with a lighter architecture is chosen so that compression is achieved while maintaining high-quality results. In common setups, distillation focuses only on final predictions, despite the fact that the student could also gain from supervision applied to internal components. Motivated by this observation, we investigate distillation targeted at intermediate layers. Because a one-to-one mapping between student and teacher layers may not exist, prior methods omit some teacher layers and perform distillation from only a subset, which adversely affects performance. To address this, we present a combinatorial mechanism that uses attention to aggregate teacher-side information, weighing the importance of each teacher layer, and then distills from these combined teacher representations into student layers. We applied the proposed method to compress a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer student models and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results indicate that the combinatorial, attention-based approach outperforms other existing techniques.

author: Cameron
title: On the Role of Pre-training for Compact Language Models
abstract: Advances in natural language representations have coincided with very large, resource-intensive models that exploit massive amounts of general-domain text via self-supervised pre-training. Because applying these models to downstream tasks is costly, a variety of compression techniques targeting pre-trained language representations have been proposed. Surprisingly, the straightforward baseline of pre-training smaller architectures and then fine-tuning them has received little attention. We first demonstrate that pre-training continues to matter for compact architectures, and that fine-tuning compact models that were pre-trained can match or exceed more complex approaches introduced in concurrent work. Building from pre-trained compact models, we investigate transferring task-specific information from large, fine-tuned models using standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm (the proposed algorithm) yields additional gains. Across a wide set of experiments, we systematically analyze how pre-training and distillation interact along two factors that have been understudied: model size and characteristics of unlabeled task data. A notable finding is that these factors produce a compound effect even when the techniques are applied sequentially to the same unlabeled data. To facilitate follow-up work, we will release our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models to the community.

author: Parsons
title: Curriculum-driven Optimization for Distillation of Dense Retrieval
abstract: It has recently been demonstrated that distilling ranking information from an existing base re-ranking model can yield more effective dense retrieval models. We introduce a general curriculum-learning optimization framework — the proposed method — that regulates the difficulty of the training instances supplied by the re-ranking (teacher) model. The proposed method trains the dense retrieval (student) model in an iterative manner, exposing it to knowledge distillation data of gradually increasing difficulty. Concretely, training starts by presenting the student with coarse-grained preference pairs derived from the teacher's ranking, and then advances toward stricter, finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. We implement a straightforward instantiation of the proposed method to improve two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Results on three public passage retrieval datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

author: Perez
title: Multi-Task Distillation for Natural Language Understanding
abstract: Training multi-task neural networks so they outperform or even match single-task models is often difficult. To address this, we apply knowledge distillation in which single-task teachers instruct a multi-task student. We add a novel gradual annealing of the teacher signal that shifts training from distillation to supervised learning, enabling the multi-task model to surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate the proposal by fine-tuning BERT jointly on the GLUE benchmark. Across tasks, our approach yields consistent improvements relative to both standard single-task and multi-task training.

author: Stewart
title: Model Compression with Privacy Guarantees through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: The growing need for intelligent mobile applications motivates placing powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on end devices. Yet the state-of-the-art accuracy of DNNs comes from ever larger and more complex architectures, producing computational demands that far exceed the resources available on mobile hardware. Compounding this, service providers must often gather and exploit large amounts of users' data, which can contain sensitive information, to construct these high-capacity models; deploying such trained models directly on public mobile devices therefore creates substantial privacy risk. To enable on-device deep learning while addressing both capacity and privacy limitations, we develop a private model compression framework, hereafter referred to as the proposed method. Following the knowledge distillation paradigm, the proposed method jointly employs hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to produce a compact and fast neural network. The knowledge transferred from the cumbersome model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed to enforce differential privacy. We also introduce a query sample selection method that is simple and effective for reducing the number of queries and for controlling the privacy loss. A suite of empirical evaluations together with an implementation on an Android mobile device demonstrate that the proposed method can compress large models efficiently while offering strong privacy guarantees. For instance, on SVHN, under a meaningful (9.83,10^{-6})-differential privacy guarantee, the compact model obtained by the proposed method achieves a 20× compression ratio and a 19× speed-up with only 0.97% accuracy loss.

author: Adams
title: Are Label Smoothing and Knowledge Distillation Fundamentally Incompatible? An Empirical Study
abstract: We undertake an empirical investigation to clarify a recently proposed viewpoint that knowledge distillation and label smoothing may be incompatible. To motivate why this concern arises, we first describe how label smoothing can remove the relative relationships encoded in teacher logits. We then establish a novel connection that characterizes the way label smoothing alters the distributions of semantically similar versus dissimilar classes. Next, we define a metric that quantitatively captures the amount of information erased from a sample's representation. By performing large-scale analyses, visualizations, and comprehensive experiments on Neural Machine Translation, Image Classification, and Binary Networks, we probe the incompatibility view's one-sidedness and imperfection. Finally, we provide a broad discussion of the conditions under which label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

author: Clark
title: A model-agnostic approach to federated learning based on knowledge distillation
abstract: Can one develop a universal API for federated learning that enables an ad-hoc collection of data-holders (agents) to collaborate and carry out federated learning? Such an API must be model-agnostic — i.e., make no assumption about the model architectures used by agents — and it cannot depend on access to representative public data. Knowledge distillation (KD) seems the natural mechanism for constructing protocols that meet these requirements. However, surprisingly, we demonstrate that most straightforward KD-based federated learning schemes exhibit poor performance. To understand this phenomenon, we introduce a theoretical framework built on a federated kernel ridge regression formulation that models both model heterogeneity and data heterogeneity. Our analysis indicates that the bulk of the performance drop is principally attributable to an inherent limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We then validate this framework by analyzing and designing new KD-based protocols; their behavior on real-world experiments with neural networks, while still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

author: Hahn
title: A unified distillation approach for object detection leveraging the Pearson Correlation Coefficient (the proposed method)
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to train smaller models for object detection. Despite this prevalence, there has been little work on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In our empirical study we observe that improved FPN features produced by a heterogeneous teacher can benefit the student even when their detection heads and label assignments differ. Directly matching feature maps for detector distillation, however, faces two difficulties. First, mismatched feature magnitudes between teacher and student could force the student into excessively strict constraints. Second, teacher FPN stages and channels with large magnitudes can dominate the gradients from the distillation loss, drowning out signals from other features in KD and introducing considerable noise. To address these issues, the proposed method aligns features using the Pearson Correlation Coefficient so as to capture relational information from the teacher while relaxing constraints on absolute magnitude. The approach consistently outperforms existing detection KD techniques, applies to cases where student and teacher are homogeneous or heterogeneous, and also converges faster. With a strong MaskRCNN-Swin teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS obtain 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which correspond to improvements of 4.1% and 4.8% over the baseline, respectively.

author: Walter
title: Distillation with a Stronger Teacher
abstract: Prior distillation work typically examines baseline scenarios in which teacher models and training strategies are not as strong or competitive with state-of-the-art approaches; in contrast, this paper presents the proposed method to distill from a stronger teacher. We empirically find that the discrepancy of predictions between the student and a stronger teacher may tend to be fairly severe. Consequently, forcing an exact correspondence of predictions using KL divergence would disturb the training and cause existing methods to perform poorly. We demonstrate that it is sufficient to preserve the relational structure among teacher and student predictions, and introduce a correlation-based loss to explicitly capture the intrinsic inter-class relations provided by the teacher. Moreover, recognizing that individual instances differ in their semantic similarity to each class, we further extend this relational matching down to the intra-class level. The proposed method is simple yet practical; extensive experiments show that it adapts well across various architectures, model sizes and training strategies, and can achieve state-of-the-art performance consistently on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

author: Edwards
title: Protecting Privacy in Federated Learning via an Ensemble Cross-Domain One-Shot Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) refers to a machine learning setup in which local nodes keep training data decentralized while jointly training a central model. To handle unbalanced data distribution, prior FL approaches commonly exchange model parameters or rely on co-distillation; these strategies, however, introduce communication bottlenecks and, more importantly, carry risks of privacy leakage. In this work, we present a privacy-preserving and communication-efficient approach in the FL setting that performs one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. The proposed method builds a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions produced by completely trained local models, providing stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms, yielding superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

author: Rios
title: Applying Knowledge Distillation to Enhance Neural Topic Models
abstract: Researchers frequently use topic models to extract human-interpretable topics that aid interpretation of large document collections. We apply knowledge distillation to fuse complementary strengths of probabilistic topic models, together with pretrained transformers. Our modular procedure is straightforward to apply to any neural topic model and yields improved topic quality; we validate this on two models with disparate architectures and achieve state-of-the-art topic coherence. We further show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

author: Foster
title: Distillation from Multiple Teachers for CTR Prediction
abstract: In recent work, deep learning-based approaches for click-through rate (CTR) prediction have been extensively investigated and have yielded improved prediction accuracy across many industrial applications. Nevertheless, much prior effort centers on constructing increasingly complex network architectures to better model sophisticated feature interactions and dynamic user behaviors. This rising architectural complexity may slow down online inference and hinder adoption in real-time applications. Rather than further complicating models, we focus on a training paradigm built on knowledge distillation (KD). KD is a teacher-student learning framework that transfers knowledge from a teacher model to a student model. Employing KD lets us reduce the student to a vanilla DNN model while still producing significant accuracy improvements over the state-of-the-art teacher models. These advantages encourage us to investigate leveraging a powerful ensemble of teachers to produce a more accurate student. We introduce additional techniques to support ensembled CTR prediction, including a gating mechanism over the teachers and early stopping guided by the distillation loss. We carry out comprehensive experiments comparing to 12 existing models on three industrial datasets. Both offline evaluations and online A/B testing demonstrate the effectiveness of our KD-based training strategy.

author: Rocha
title: Few Shot Network Compression with Layer-wise Distillation
abstract: Model compression is widely used to produce light-weight deep neural networks. However, most prevalent methods require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, a need that can be at odds with privacy and security concerns. As a trade-off between privacy and performance, this paper studies few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can one compress a network while incurring negligible performance drop? The principal difficulty in this setting stems from large estimation errors during inference originating from the original network, since the compressed network can easily over-fit the few training instances. Such estimation errors may propagate and accumulate layer-wisely, ultimately degrading the final output. To address this issue, we present a layer-wise knowledge distillation approach as the proposed method. By interweaving hidden layers of the teacher and student network, the layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced. The proposed method constitutes a general framework that is compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are provided.

author: Ellis
title: Distilling Representation Knowledge into Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Knowledge distillation is a framework for improving resource-efficient graph neural networks by leveraging larger, more expressive teacher models. Prior distillation work for GNNs introduced a local structure preserving objective that enforces agreement between teacher and student on edge-level structural relationships among node embeddings. In this paper we examine whether targeting the teacher's global embedding topology yields a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, motivated by the presence of latent interactions and noisy edges in many real-world graphs. We develop the proposed method: a contrastive representation distillation scheme that uses contrastive learning to implicitly retain global topology by aligning student node embeddings with teacher node embeddings within a common representation space. We also assemble an expanded suite of benchmarks drawn from large-scale real-world datasets where the gap in performance between teacher and student GNNs is appreciable. Evaluation on 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures shows that the proposed method reliably improves the accuracy and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming the local structure preserving loss (and a variant of that loss adapted to preserve global structure) as well as distillation baselines ported from 2D computer vision. A representational similarity analysis between teacher and student embedding spaces indicates that the proposed method achieves a balance between preserving local and global relationships, whereas structure-preserving approaches tend to preserve one type of relationship at the expense of the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

author: Baker
title: Recovering Low-Frequency Words: Maximizing Parallel Data Use for Non-Autoregressive Translation
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely employed to generate synthetic parallel examples for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, a mismatch on low-frequency words between the distilled corpus and the original parallel data persists, which results in increased errors when predicting those low-frequency words. To mitigate this issue, we allow NAT models to see authentic data directly by exploiting pretraining. Through an examination of directed alignments, we observe that KD makes alignments from low-frequency source words to targets more deterministic, while it does not produce a sufficient number of alignments from low-frequency target words back to source. In response, we introduce the proposed method that revitalizes additional alignments for low-frequency target words. To fully leverage both authentic and synthetic examples, we merge these complementary techniques into a unified training strategy aimed at further improving NAT. Experiments are carried out on five translation benchmarks using two advanced architectures. The results show that the proposed approach can significantly and universally enhance translation quality by lowering translation errors on low-frequency words. Notably, the method attains 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU on WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT.

author: Wright
title: The proposed method for comprehensive scene understanding from videos
abstract: Complete perception of the environment is critical for autonomous systems. Prior work has shown that deep neural networks can recover geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) using only a monocular video stream, without any explicit supervision from ground truth annotations, which are particularly difficult to obtain for these two tasks. Here we advance toward holistic scene understanding with monocular cameras by training a model to produce depth and motion jointly with semantics; supervision for semantics is supplied via proxy ground truth images generated by a pre-trained network through distillation. We tackle the three tasks together by a) introducing a novel training protocol grounded in knowledge distillation and self-supervision and b) designing a compact network architecture that permits efficient scene understanding when executed on power hungry GPUs as well as on low-power embedded platforms. We perform a thorough evaluation of the proposed framework and demonstrate that it achieves state-of-the-art results for monocular depth estimation, optical flow and motion segmentation.

author: Hoffman
title: Distillation-based strategies for federated learning
abstract: Many distributed training setups avoid sending raw data between participants and instead share model parameters. A canonical instance is federated learning, where workers communicate gradients or weights of their neural network models. When communication bandwidth is constrained, however, parameter exchange becomes prohibitively expensive, especially for modern deep neural networks that contain an enormous number of model parameters. To address this bottleneck, the proposed method transmits only model outputs, whose dimensionality is typically far smaller than the full model (for example, 10 labels for the MNIST dataset). The objective of this chapter is to develop a thorough understanding of the proposed method while showing its reductions in communication and its relevance across multiple problems. Toward elucidating how the proposed method operates, the first portion of the chapter delivers a novel asymptotic analysis for two core algorithms underlying the proposed method — knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD) — by leveraging the theory of the neural tangent kernel (NTK). The second portion describes a baseline implementation of the proposed method for a classification problem and reports its accuracy and communication-efficiency trade-offs relative to federated learning. Finally, to illustrate the broader applicability of the proposed method, the last portion examines two example use cases: operation over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and application to reinforcement learning.

author: Baker
title: Combining Heterogeneous Classifiers through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: We consider the task of merging the knowledge held by multiple classifiers that vary in architecture and in which target classes they cover, with the goal of producing a single classifier when only a generic collection of unlabelled examples is available. This problem arises when data are collected across multiple parties that cannot exchange raw examples—for instance because of privacy constraints—and where only locally trained models can be shared. Moreover, different parties may be unable to gather examples for every class and may be restricted to distinct classification models by their computational budgets. To address this setting, we generalise knowledge distillation to combine heterogeneous classifiers into one student model. We derive a probabilistic connection between the outputs of these heterogeneous classifiers and the full probability distribution over all classes. Exploiting this relation, we develop two families of methods—one based on cross-entropy minimisation and the other on matrix factorisation—that permit estimation of soft labels over the entire label set from unlabelled inputs and use them as surrogate targets to train a unified classifier. Extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 show that the proposed approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

author: Richards
title: Text generation through knowledge distillation and generative adversarial networks
abstract: Generating text is central to many NLP tasks, including language modeling, machine translation and summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have produced impressive, high-quality image results in computer vision, and have more recently attracted substantial interest within the NLP community. Replicating that level of success for language is expected to be more challenging because of the discrete nature of text. In this paper, the proposed method leverages knowledge distillation to make the GAN framework effective for text generation. We show that autoencoders (AEs) provide a continuous sentence representation — a smooth encoding that assigns non-zero probabilities to more than one word — and we distill that encoding so the generator is trained to synthesize comparable smooth representations. A set of experiments on different datasets validates the idea and demonstrates that the proposed approach attains superior performance by BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

author: Hurst
title: Distillation for Ranking: Training Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender Systems
abstract: We introduce a new procedure to train ranking models for recommender systems that yields both effectiveness and efficiency. Knowledge distillation (KD) has been demonstrated successful in image recognition at producing models that are accurate while being compact. We propose a KD approach tailored to learning-to-rank tasks, hereafter called the proposed method. Concretely, a smaller student model is trained to rank documents/items using supervision from the original training data together with guidance provided by a larger teacher model. The student obtains ranking performance comparable to the large teacher, while its reduced model size makes online inference more efficient. The proposed method is flexible since it is orthogonal to the selection of ranking models used for teacher and student. We address the specific challenges of applying distillation in ranking settings. Experiments on public data sets and with state-of-the-art recommendation models confirm the intended outcome: the student trained with the proposed method has a model size less than half of the teacher, achieves ranking performance similar to the teacher, and is much better than the student trained without the proposed distillation.

author: Ross
title: Distillation from an Ensemble into NMT
abstract: Translating a sentence with a Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine incurs high time costs, and reducing model size accelerates that process. Knowledge distillation defines a procedure for training a student network to attain better performance by learning from a stronger teacher network. We show that the translation quality provided by an ensemble teacher and by an oracle BLEU teacher network can be transferred into a single NMT system. In addition, we obtain translation improvements when the teacher network has the same architecture and dimensions as the student network. Because training the student model remains expensive, we propose a data filtering method that exploits the knowledge of the teacher model; this not only speeds up the training but also leads to better translation quality. The techniques require no code change and can be straightforwardly reproduced with any NMT architecture to speed up the decoding process.

author: Robinson
title: Analyzing and Enhancing Lexical Choice for Non-Autoregressive Translation
abstract: Training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models commonly relies on knowledge distillation (KD), where an autoregressive teacher model simplifies the raw data. We empirically demonstrate that a collateral effect of this process is that the teacher transfers its lexical choice mistakes affecting low-frequency words into the NAT student. To address this, we advocate exposing NAT models to the original raw data so that information about low-frequency words, which is omitted by distillation, can be recovered. Concretely, we incorporate an auxiliary Kullback-Leibler divergence term that compares the NAT model's lexical preferences with those encoded in the raw data. Experiments over multiple language pairs and model architectures show the effectiveness and broad applicability of the proposed method. In-depth analyses corroborate that the gains arise from reducing lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Notably, the approach pushes SOTA NAT performance to 27.8 BLEU on WMT14 English-German and 33.8 BLEU on WMT16 Romanian-English. We will release the source code.

author: Bright
title: Enabling practical lipreading via distilled, resource-efficient models
abstract: Recent advances in lipreading have been driven by renewed progress in neural networks. Prior work has focused on choices such as finding better architectures or improving generalization, yet a substantial gap remains between those approaches and the demands of deploying lipreading in real settings. We present a collection of contributions that markedly narrow this gap: first, using self-distillation we push the state-of-the-art on LRW and LRW-1000 to 88.5% and 46.6%, respectively, representing a wide improvement. Second, we introduce several architectural revisions, including a novel depthwise separable temporal convolutional network head, which reduces computational cost to only a small fraction of the already efficient baseline model. Third, we show that knowledge distillation is highly effective at recovering accuracy for the lightweight variants. The outcome is a family of models spanning multiple accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. Importantly, our best lightweight configurations achieve parity with the current state-of-the-art while offering reductions of 8.2x and 3.9x in computational cost and number of parameters, respectively, which we hope will enable deployment of lipreading models in practical applications.

author: Hicks
title: The proposed method for knowledge transfer: Teaching models to adapt
abstract: When training and test distributions differ, domain adaptation is essential for many practical applications. Current deep learning solutions typically require joint training on source and target data, which is impractical when models must be adapted to numerous domains or to domains that change over time (for example, spam detection where attackers continually alter their tactics). To address this limitation, the proposed method adapts Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation setting. We demonstrate that a student model that exploits the domain-specific expertise of several teachers and weights them according to inter-domain similarity attains state-of-the-art results for unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark. In the single-teacher case, relying on domain similarity alone to assess a teacher’s trustworthiness is insufficient. We therefore introduce a simple metric that shows strong correlation with a teacher’s accuracy on the target domain. Selecting high-confidence target examples according to this metric and using them in training allows the student to reach state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

author: Williams
title: Zero-shot teacher-to-student transfer using the proposed method
abstract: Training a compact student to emulate a larger teacher is a standard objective in deep learning. Yet, with dataset sizes growing and privacy constraints tightening, the training examples that informed the teacher are often not accessible. We present a novel procedure that trains a student to reproduce its teacher's predictions without relying on any data or metadata. The core mechanism is an adversarial generator that synthesizes images which reveal where the student's outputs diverge from the teacher's; those synthesized samples are then employed to update the student. The resulting student closely approximates the teacher on SVHN, and on CIFAR10 our approach outperforms prior state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation when provided 100 images per class, even though no real data are used. We also propose a metric that measures belief alignment between teacher and student in the vicinity of decision boundaries, and find a significantly higher match for the zero-shot student versus a student distilled with real data. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

author: Rodriguez
title: Capturing and Extending the Knowledge Encoded by Graph Neural Networks via an Effective Knowledge Distillation Framework
abstract: Semi-supervised learning on graphs remains a significant challenge in machine learning. Recently, graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as state-of-the-art classification techniques and have demonstrated superiority over more classical approaches such as label propagation. Nevertheless, the complex architectures of these neural approaches produce intricate prediction procedures that may fail to fully exploit useful prior information present in the data, for example that structurally correlated nodes are likely to share a class label. To tackle these shortcomings, we introduce a framework grounded in knowledge distillation. The proposed method extracts the knowledge contained in any pre-trained GNN (teacher model) and transfers it into a purpose-built student model. The student employs two straightforward prediction mechanisms—label propagation and feature transformation—which explicitly retain structure-based and feature-based prior knowledge, respectively. Concretely, we construct the student as a trainable mixture of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation components. Consequently, the trained student leverages both the prior knowledge and the information distilled from GNN teachers to produce more effective predictions. The student’s decision process is also more interpretable than that of typical GNNs. We evaluate the approach on five public benchmark datasets, using seven GNNs as teachers: GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII and GLP. Results indicate that the distilled student consistently outperforms its corresponding teacher by 1.4% - 4.7% on average. Code and data are available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF

author: Burton
title: Making transformer-based large-scale language representations efficient by the proposed hardware-friendly block-structured pruning
abstract: Large-scale language models pre-trained on vast corpora have progressively attained strong accuracy across many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Yet constrained weight storage and limited computational throughput on hardware platforms have restricted the practical adoption of these pre-trained models, particularly for edge computing. We present the proposed method: an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation that applies hardware-friendly block-structured pruning. For optimization, we integrate the reweighted group Lasso into the block-structured pruning procedure. In addition to substantially reducing weight storage and computation, the proposed approach delivers high compression rates. On the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks, experiments with multiple models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) demonstrate that we obtain up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). The proposed method is orthogonal to compact pre-trained models produced via knowledge distillation, such as DistilBERT: applying our method on top of DistilBERT yields a further 1.79x average compression rate with zero or minor accuracy degradation. This makes the final compressed model suitable for deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.

author: Conner
title: Distilling Task-Specific Knowledge from BERT into Compact Student Networks
abstract: Neural networks in natural language processing have moved toward increased depth and sophistication. BERT, ELMo, and GPT serve as prominent examples of these deep language representation models. As a result, many have taken the stance that earlier, shallower architectures for language understanding are effectively obsolete. In this work, however, we show that very simple, lightweight neural networks can still be made competitive without architecture changes, external training data, or additional input features. The proposed method distills knowledge from BERT, a state-of-the-art language representation model, into a single-layer BiLSTM and into a siamese variant for sentence-pair tasks. Across multiple datasets spanning paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification, the student obtains results comparable with ELMo while using roughly 100 times fewer parameters and about 15 times less inference time.

author: Henderson
title: Removing Graph Dependency: Enhancing MLPs via Knowledge Distillation from GNNs
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely used in graph machine learning and deliver strong performance on broad node classification problems. However, their adoption in real-world production is hindered by scalability issues stemming from data dependency: GNN inference requires accessing neighbor nodes multiple hops away from a target, and retrieving those neighbors imposes costs that conflict with latency-constrained applications. Approaches that accelerate inference such as pruning and quantization reduce Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations and thus speed up GNNs, but they offer limited gains because they do not remove the underlying data dependency. In contrast, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) lack graph dependency and perform inference much faster than GNNs, although they typically achieve lower node-classification accuracy. Motivated by these complementary trade-offs, we unite GNNs and MLPs through knowledge distillation (KD). We demonstrate that applying GNN-to-MLP KD yields large improvements in MLP performance. The resulting distilled MLPs have no inference graph dependency. Models obtained this way that reach competitive accuracy run inference faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration techniques by 14X-27X. In a production-like evaluation covering both transductive and inductive predictions on 7 datasets, these distilled MLPs outperform stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and attain parity with GNNs on 6/7 datasets. A thorough analysis characterizes when and why the distilled MLPs can match GNN accuracy, and recommends them as a practical option for latency-sensitive deployments.

author: Brown
title: A unified framework for compressing vision transformers
abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have seen rapidly increasing adoption. When trained on very large datasets, ViTs can attain competitive performance despite not employing customized image operators like convolutions. Their computational cost, however, remains prohibitive because of repeatedly stacking multi-head self-attention modules and other components. In contrast to the extensive literature and demonstrated success in compressing convolutional neural networks, work on Vision Transformer compression has only recently begun, and prior efforts generally address only one or two compression avenues. We present the proposed method, a unified ViT compression framework that integrates three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. Concretely, we pose a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization formulation that jointly learns model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations under a distillation loss. The resulting constrained optimization is solved via the primal-dual algorithm. We evaluate on several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and the proposed method consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed to 50% of the original FLOPs with almost no loss in accuracy. Codes are available online: https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC.

author: James
title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning via the Proposed Method
abstract: The learning objective used by CLIP in its vision-language setting does not adequately handle the noisy many-to-many correspondences present in web-harvested image-caption corpora, and this deficiency contributes to inefficiencies in both compute and data. To mitigate this problem, we present a novel training framework grounded in cross-modal contrastive learning that combines the proposed method with soft image-text alignments to learn robust representations from noisy data more efficiently. The proposed method distills its own knowledge to dynamically produce soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in each minibatch, and those targets are employed to update model parameters. Comprehensive evaluation on 14 benchmark datasets demonstrates that the proposed method consistently outperforms the corresponding CLIP baseline across multiple settings — (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval — without incurring additional computational cost. Experiments on an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed indicate that the proposed method yields superior effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Finally, pretraining on datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that the improvements over CLIP tend to scale with the number of training examples.

author: Ferrell
title: Improving Supernet Training via Adaptive Alpha-Divergence
abstract: Weight-sharing NAS is a practical approach for automating the design of efficient neural architectures. In this paradigm a supernet is constructed that contains candidate architectures as sub-networks, and the supernet together with its sub-networks are trained jointly. The effectiveness of weight-sharing NAS depends critically on distilling knowledge from the supernet into its sub-networks. We observe that the commonly used distillation divergence, KL divergence, can cause student sub-networks to either over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, which in turn harms sub-network performance. To address this, we replace the standard divergence with a more general alpha-divergence for supernet training. By choosing the alpha-divergence adaptively, the proposed method prevents both over-estimation and under-estimation of the teacher model uncertainty. We integrate the alpha-divergence based training into both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS and report substantial gains. Concretely, the discovered model family produced by the proposed method surpasses prior-art models across a wide set of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We obtain ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available.

author: Rice
title: The proposed method: Generalization of Fake Media Detection through Continual Representation and Distillation
abstract: Artificial intelligence has advanced markedly over recent decades, yet it remains largely dependent on fixed datasets and stationary environments. Continual learning is a growing field that studies how systems can acquire knowledge sequentially from a continuous stream of correlated data in the same way that biological systems do. At the same time, fake media — in particular deepfakes and synthetic face images — have become highly relevant to modern multimedia technologies. Recently, numerous methods have been proposed that detect deepfakes with high accuracy. However, these approaches suffer significantly from their dependence on fixed datasets evaluated under limited settings. To address this, we apply continual learning to the learning dynamics of neural networks, stressing its capacity to increase data efficiency significantly. We present the proposed method, which integrates the concepts of Continual Learning (CL), Representation Learning (RL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD). The proposed method is designed to carry out sequential domain adaptation tasks on new deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets while effectively minimizing catastrophic forgetting in a teacher-student model setting. Extensive experimental results show that the proposed method efficiently adapts across domains to detect low-quality deepfake videos and GAN-generated images drawn from multiple datasets, outperforming the state-of-the-art baseline methods.

author: Maddox
title: Many-to-Many Layer Alignment Using Earth Mover's Distance for Compressing BERT
abstract: Pre-trained language models such as BERT deliver strong results across natural language processing (NLP) tasks, but their large storage and computational requirements impede deployment on resource-constrained devices. We present the proposed method, a BERT distillation approach that implements many-to-many layer mapping so that any intermediate student layer may receive supervision from any intermediate teacher layers. This design is motivated by the intuition that different NLP tasks demand different amounts of linguistic knowledge distributed across BERT's intermediate layers, and the flexible mapping lets the student adaptively draw from distinct teacher layers for varied tasks. To realize the matching between teacher and student, we employ Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to compute the minimal cumulative cost required to transfer knowledge from the teacher network to the student network; EMD thus enables effective matching for many-to-many layer mapping. EMD is also applicable when layers differ in size and provides a measure of semantic distance between the teacher network and student network. In addition, we introduce a cost attention mechanism that automatically learns the layer weights used in the EMD calculation, which is intended to further improve performance and accelerate convergence. Extensive experiments on the GLUE benchmark demonstrate that the proposed method achieves competitive performance compared to strong competitors in terms of both accuracy and model compression.

author: Valencia
title: A Survey of Compression Techniques for Deep Learning Models Applied to Text
abstract: Recent years have seen substantial advances in natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) driven by deep learning approaches such as Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs), together with Transformer [120]-based systems including Generative Pre-training Transformer (GPT-2) [94], Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [24], Extra-Long Network (XLNet) [134], Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5) [95], T-NLG [98], GShard [63] and Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) [73]. Nevertheless, the parameter footprints of these models remain humongous. At the same time, practical deployments demand small model size, low response times and low computational power wattage. This survey examines six classes of compression methods — Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Tensor Decomposition, Parameter Sharing, and Sub-quadratic Transformer based methods — for reducing such models to enable their use in real industry NLP projects. Given the urgent need for compact, efficient applications and the large volume of recent work, we believe this survey organizes the extensive contributions from the deep learning for NLP community over the past few years into a coherent story.

author: Smith
title: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Compressing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has recently attracted interest because of the growing need to run GANs on mobile devices for many applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. Yet, in contrast to the extensive work on compressing other deep models, efforts aimed at GAN compression (typically focusing on the generators) are still at an early stage. Current GAN compression techniques tend to be restricted to particular GAN architectures and loss formulations. Motivated by the recent advances of AutoML for deep compression, we apply AutoML to GAN compression and design the proposed framework. Beginning from a specially constructed efficient search space, the proposed method carries out an end-to-end discovery of new efficient generators subject to target computational resource constraints. This search is steered by the original GAN through knowledge distillation to accomplish the compression objective. The proposed method is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and broadly applicable across GAN models. We test it on two representative tasks, image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, the proposed method produces remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our code and pretrained models are available online.

author: Le
title: Rethinking Video-Pose embeddings for understanding Activities of Daily Living with the proposed method
abstract: A large body of work has focused on fusing RGB and 3D poses to recognize Activities of Daily Living (ADL). Many ADL classes are visually similar and require modeling fine-grained cues to separate them. Because recent 3D ConvNets are too rigid to capture subtle visual patterns that unfold across an action, the literature is dominated by approaches that combine RGB and 3D Poses. However, deriving 3D poses from an RGB stream is costly when dedicated sensors are absent, which constrains deployment in low-latency real-world settings. How can 3D Poses be exploited most effectively for ADL recognition? To answer this, we introduce an extension of a pose-driven attention mechanism — the proposed method — and pursue two complementary directions. The first direction transfers Pose knowledge into RGB via feature-level distillation; the second direction imitates pose-driven attention through attention-level distillation. These two distillation strategies are then merged into a unified model (the proposed method). We demonstrate that the proposed method is not only effective but also yields a high speed up and exhibits high resilience to noisy Poses. The proposed method, evaluated with or without 3D Poses, outperforms representative baselines on 4 public datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

author: Maldonado
title: Training Students by Imitating Teacher Features
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a widely used approach for training compact networks (the "student") under supervision from larger models (the "teacher"). Existing approaches typically employ the teacher's soft logits as auxiliary supervision for training the student. We contend that targeting the teacher's features at the penultimate layer for imitation is more beneficial. Besides enabling the student to capture more effective information directly from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can be applied even when the teacher was trained without a softmax layer. Empirical results indicate this approach attains higher accuracy than traditional KD. To better support feature mimicking, we factor each feature vector into its magnitude and its direction. We argue the teacher should allow greater freedom in the student feature magnitudes while encouraging the student to concentrate on matching feature directions. To enforce this behavior, we introduce a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With this loss the proposed method more precisely matches feature directions, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We present theoretical analyses of how LSH helps direction matching, and extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

author: Herrera
title: Reducing the Size of GANs via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are employed in machine learning for tasks including super resolution, domain transfer, and creation of synthetic datasets. Contemporary high-performing GAN architectures frequently contain on the order of tens of millions of parameters, which raises the cost of deploying them on low-SWAP platforms (size, weight, and power) such as mobile devices and in situations that require real-time operation. To our knowledge, prior work has not focused on decreasing the parameter count of GANs. The proposed method applies knowledge distillation so that a compact "student" GAN is trained to imitate a larger "teacher" GAN. When applied to MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A, the distillation achieves compression ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1 respectively, while preserving the quality of generated images. Our experiments indicate a qualitative limit to GAN compression. Moreover, given the same parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained with standard training methods. We conjecture this benefit is partly due to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs, which permits efficient optimization via alternating gradient descent. Hence, training an over-parameterized GAN and then applying the proposed compression produces a small-parameter generative model of high quality.

author: Davidson
title: Robust Re-Identification via Distillation from Multiple Views
abstract: Robustness in Re-Identification is commonly obtained by exploiting tracking cues in a Video-To-Video pipeline. Such approaches, however, suffer a substantial performance collapse when handling single-image queries, as in the Image-To-Video scenario. Prior work mitigates this degradation by conveying temporal information from a Video-based network into an Image-based model. Here, we introduce a training scheme that enables the transfer of richer knowledge originating from a collection of views of the target. The proposed method encodes this visual variability as a supervision signal inside a teacher-student distillation setup, where a teacher that has access to multiple views instructs a student exposed to fewer views. As a consequence, the student exceeds both its teacher and the existing state-of-the-art for Image-To-Video by a large margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId and 5% on VeRi-776). We present an extensive study — across Person, Vehicle and Animal Re-ID — that examines the characteristics of the proposed method from qualitative and quantitative viewpoints. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

author: Rodriguez
title: Publishing Graph Neural Networks under Differential Privacy
abstract: As graph neural networks (GNNs) gain traction in privacy-sensitive domains such as healthcare and medicine, concerns about the confidentiality of trained GNNs have intensified. In particular, GNNs remain susceptible to privacy attacks, for example membership inference attacks, even when adversaries possess only black-box access. We introduce the proposed framework, a privacy-preserving pipeline for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming availability of a public unlabeled graph, the proposed framework outputs GNNs trained explicitly on public data while also transferring knowledge derived from private data in a privacy-preserving manner. The proposed framework integrates the knowledge-distillation framework with two noise mechanisms, random subsampling and noisy labeling, to obtain rigorous privacy guarantees. We analyze the method theoretically in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Empirically, we demonstrate strong experimental performance compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Code for the proposed framework is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/graph-privacy-code.

author: Graham
title: Proposed Regularization for Federated Learning
abstract: Client-side data heterogeneity and imbalance present a major obstacle in federated learning, producing divergence among local networks and destabilizing convergence of the global model. To address these limitations, the proposed method applies an architectural regularization that inserts multiple auxiliary branches into each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks across several layers, and it uses online knowledge distillation to align the representations of the main pathway with those of the auxiliary hybrid pathways. This design makes the global model more robust even in the non-iid setting and can be integrated into various federated learning frameworks without incurring extra communication costs. We conduct comprehensive empirical studies and report remarkable performance gains in accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. We release the source code on our project page.

author: Chavez
title: Knowledge distillation without training data for deep neural networks
abstract: Recent progress in model compression has produced techniques that reduce the footprint of large neural networks to only a small fraction of their original size while maintaining the bulk, and in some cases virtually all, of their accuracy. A common requirement of these techniques is availability of the original training set, which is not always feasible when the teacher model was fit on very large collections or when releasing those data would create privacy or safety risks, for instance in biometrics applications. We introduce the proposed method for data-free knowledge distillation, which can compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets down to a fraction of their size using only limited additional metadata supplied alongside a pretrained model release. We evaluate several types of metadata that can be used with the proposed method and characterize the tradeoffs associated with each choice.

author: Mckay
title: The proposed method: Towards efficient distillation of large-scale language models
abstract: Recent large-scale language models achieve strong empirical performance. However, these gains come with larger model sizes, increased power consumption, and slower inference, limiting their use on low-resource platforms with constrained memory and computation. Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective framework for compressing such large models. At the same time, large-scale neural networks are prone to memorizing training examples and therefore can produce unstable predictions under small distribution shifts. Moreover, when task-specific data is scarce, the student model has limited opportunities to obtain useful signals from the teacher. To address these challenges, we present the proposed method, a data-agnostic distillation framework that leverages mixup, a simple yet efficient data augmentation technique, to strengthen the distilled model’s generalization. Concretely, besides the original training samples, the student is trained to imitate the teacher’s behavior on linear interpolations of example pairs. From a theoretical perspective, we prove that under reasonable conditions the proposed method yields a smaller gap between generalization error and empirical error. Empirically, on the GLUE benchmark the proposed method consistently produces significant gains over standard KD training and outperforms several competitive baselines. Experiments in limited-data settings and ablation studies further corroborate the advantages of the proposed approach.

author: Liu
title: Granting Multimodal Generation to CLIP through the Proposed Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream models such as CLIP, carried out on very large collections of image–text pairings, has demonstrated superior performance on multimodal alignment tasks. Despite these strengths, the resulting systems lack the ability to perform multimodal generative work because the text encoder remains weak. To address this shortcoming, we augment the dual-stream VLP model by integrating a pre-trained textual language model (PLM) via the proposed vision-language knowledge distillation, thereby enabling multimodal generation. This distillation procedure is pretty data- and computation-efficient relative to training from scratch. Empirical evaluation shows the distilled model attains strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation problems, including open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For instance, it obtains 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, outperforming the prior state-of-the-art zero-shot model while using 7× fewer parameters. Moreover, the PLM's original textual language understanding and generation capabilities are preserved after distillation, making the model useful for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

author: Mason
title: Training Portable Student Networks through Feature Embedding
abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks are used in a wide range of applications, but their substantial storage and computation demands prevent deployment on mobile devices. Knowledge distillation aims to optimize a portable student network by taking the knowledge from a well-trained heavy teacher network. Conventional teacher-student approaches have typically employed extra fully-connected layers to connect intermediate layers of the teacher and student networks, introducing a large number of auxiliary parameters. In contrast, the present work seeks to transfer information from teacher to student without adding new variables that need to be optimized. We reinterpret the teacher-student paradigm from the standpoint of feature embedding. Through the proposed locality-preserving loss, the student network is encouraged to produce low-dimensional features that inherit intrinsic properties of their corresponding high-dimensional features from the teacher network. The resulting portable network can thus naturally maintain performance on par with the teacher network. Theoretical analysis is provided to justify the lower computation complexity of the proposed method. Experiments on benchmark datasets and well-trained networks indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art teacher-student learning methods in terms of computational and storage complexity.

author: White
title: Student-teacher distilling of portable GANs for image translation
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are widely applied in many image-to-image translation tasks, but their heavy computation and storage cost make deployment on mobile devices difficult. Traditional network compression methods concentrate on visual recognition tasks and never deal with generation tasks. Drawing on knowledge distillation, we train a student generator with fewer parameters to inherit both low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To boost the student generator's capability, we introduce a student discriminator that measures distances among real images and images produced by the student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is then employed to jointly optimize the student generator and the student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models that achieve strong performance.

author: Gaines
title: Task-oriented BERT compression via differentiable Neural Architecture Search
abstract: Pre-trained large language models like BERT achieve strong performance across many natural language processing tasks. Their very large parameter counts hinder deployment in real-time settings that demand fast inference under constrained resources. Most prior compression techniques produce compact versions of BERT that are task-independent, meaning a single compressed BERT is applied to all downstream tasks. Motivated by the need and potential advantages of task-specific compression, the proposed compression method employs differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically generate task-adaptive, compact BERT variants tailored to particular tasks. We introduce a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to steer the search and an efficiency-aware loss used as search constraints, which together allow a favorable trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. Evaluation on several NLP tasks shows that the resulting task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT at inference and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

author: Harrell
title: Client-inclusive federated learning across heterogeneous devices
abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a key paradigm for training a global model from decentralized data while preserving privacy. Most existing FL methods typically assume the global model can be trained on every participating client. In practice, however, client devices are heterogeneous and present diverse computing capabilities. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, applying them in FL is challenging when some clients are weak. Simple fixes such as removing weak clients or deploying a single small model for all participants create problems: dropped clients become under-represented, and overall accuracy suffers due to data loss or the limited representation ability of a small model. In this work we present the proposed method, a client-inclusive federated learning approach that tackles these issues. The core idea is to allocate models of varying sizes to clients according to their compute capacity — larger models run on powerful clients and smaller models on weak clients. We also provide an effective mechanism to share knowledge among multiple local models of different sizes so that every client can take part in training while the final model can be big and powerful enough. In addition, we introduce a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge from big models on powerful clients to small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices within the FL framework.

author: Evans
title: Training Small-Footprint Evaluation Metrics for MT
abstract: Researchers increasingly rely on trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT to assess machine translation and multilingual text generation, casting evaluation as a regression task and building on representations produced by multilingual pre-trained models like XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Prior work on related problems suggests that top effectiveness is obtained with large models, a requirement that is expensive and often infeasible for routine evaluation. We examine the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. A suite of experiments indicates that model size is, indeed, a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer. We then show that distillation can alleviate this constraint: we leverage synthetic data generation and transfer knowledge from a single teacher into multiple students trained on related languages. The proposed method delivers up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and achieves 92.6% of RemBERT's performance while using only a third of its parameters.

author: Fowler
title: Self-supervised distillation for compact visual representation learning
abstract: This work examines self-supervised learning targeted at small models. Our empirical investigation motivates the problem: contrastive self-supervised learning, while widely adopted and able to produce substantial gains for large networks, does not perform well for small architectures. To address this shortcoming, we introduce a new learning paradigm, the proposed method, which carries out self-supervised distillation by employing a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student). Rather than learning directly from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to reproduce the distribution of similarity scores that a teacher assigns across a set of instances. Results demonstrate that the proposed method produces a dramatic improvement in small-network performance on downstream tasks. Against self-supervised baselines, on ImageNet-1k the proposed method raises top-1 accuracy on EfficientNet-B0 from 42.2% to 67.6%, and on MobileNet-v3-Large from 36.3% to 68.2%.

author: Lynch
title: Knowledge distillation from visual models to sensor-only action recognition
abstract: Multi-modal approaches to Human Activity Recognition (HAR) have recently been found to yield improved accuracy. Yet, the limited computational budget of typical wearable platforms such as smartwatches prevents those devices from running such resource-intensive techniques directly. To address this limitation, we present an end-to-end vision-to-sensor knowledge distillation framework. Under this framework, only time-series input — specifically accelerometer data — is required from the wearable at test time. Consequently, the solution decreases computational load on edge devices while producing a model whose performance closely matches that of the more expensive multi-modal teacher. To bridge the gap between temporal sensor signals and convolutional visual models, we first transform the time-series into two-dimensional images using a Gramian Angular Field (GAF) encoding. For distillation, ResNet18 serves as the teacher network and a multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception is trained as the student network. We also introduce a novel loss term that exploits distance and angular relationships to reduce modality variations between the vision and sensor domains. Extensive experiments on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD confirm the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed approach, which can be deployed on wearable sensors.

author: Hernandez
title: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field via the proposed method for Efficient Novel View Synthesis
abstract: Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) has recently demonstrated strong promise for encoding complex scenes with neural networks. A major limitation of NeRF is its costly inference: producing a single pixel’s value involves hundreds of queries to the NeRF network. Existing approaches largely focus on cutting the number of sampled points, yet they do not eliminate the underlying iterative sampling process. In contrast, Neural Light Field (NeLF) offers a more direct formulation for novel view synthesis, where evaluating a pixel can be done with a single network evaluation and without ray-marching. In this work we design a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively model the light field. We show that successful training of such a deep NeLF hinges on abundant supervision, so we transfer knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model through data distillation. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world scenes demonstrate advantages of the proposed method over alternative algorithms. On synthetic scenes we obtain 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, while producing substantially better rendering (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) than NeRF, without any customized parallelism requirement.

author: Farmer
title: Achieving Resource-Efficient 3D Object Detection through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: State-of-the-art 3D object detectors often deliver strong accuracy at the cost of substantial computational demands. In this work we examine knowledge distillation (KD) as a route to efficient 3D object detectors, with emphasis on commonly used pillar- and voxel-based detectors. Lacking established teacher-student design patterns, we begin by investigating how to derive student networks that trade off accuracy and efficiency, exploring both model compression and reductions in input resolution. Next, we assemble a benchmark for adapting KD techniques developed for 2D tasks to the 3D detection setting, evaluating them on six carefully constructed teacher-student pairs. Building on these findings, we present an improved KD pipeline that includes an enhanced logit KD procedure which applies distillation only at a small set of important spatial positions identified from the teacher classification response, together with a teacher-guided student initialization that transfers the teacher’s feature extraction ability to the student via weight inheritance. We validate the approach with extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. The best-performing student attains 65.75% LEVEL 2 mAPH, outperforming its teacher while consuming only 44% of the teacher FLOPs. The most efficient student runs at 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is 2.2× faster than PointPillar while achieving even higher accuracy. Code for the proposed method is available.

author: Ryan
title: Knowledge distillation to adapt multi-modal segmentation networks for mono-modal use
abstract: Combining multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been the subject of extensive recent work. Across a range of applications, fusing information coming from different modalities has been shown to yield higher segmentation accuracy than using a single modality. In clinical practice, however, collecting several modalities is frequently impractical because of a restricted number of physicians and scanners and because of the need to reduce costs and scan duration; typically only one modality is available. In this work we introduce the proposed method, a framework that transfers knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal network (student). The proposed method implements an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework in which the student is trained using a subset (1 modality) of the teacher’s input channels (n modalities). We validate the approach on brain tumor segmentation using the BraTS 2018 dataset. Experiments with multiple architectures demonstrate that the student network successfully absorbs information from the teacher and consistently outperforms the baseline mono-modal network with respect to segmentation accuracy.

author: Osborne
title: Knowledge-distillation from deep networks for Electronic Healthcare Records applications
abstract: The exponential expansion of Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has created both new opportunities and pressing needs for the extraction of meaningful, data-driven representations and for uncovering disease patterns within Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models frequently deliver superior results for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, yet they suffer from limited model interpretability, a characteristic that is essential for clinicians engaged in decision-making. We introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach — the proposed method — intended to learn interpretable phenotype features that preserve robust predictive ability while reproducing the predictive behavior of the deep models. Our framework employs Gradient Boosting Trees to derive interpretable features from deep learning architectures such as a Stacked Denoising Autoencoder or a Long Short-Term Memory network. Extensive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves similar or better performance compared to the deep learning approaches, and yields interpretable phenotypes to support clinical decision making.

author: Moreno
title: Training Perception-Aware Agile Quadrotor Navigation Through Cluttered Environments
abstract: Recently, neural control policies have surpassed existing model-based planning-and-control methods in accomplishing minimum-time autonomous navigation of quadrotors through cluttered environments. Nevertheless, these policies are not perception aware, which is essential in vision-based navigation because of the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated dynamics of a quadrotor. We present a learning-based system that attains perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. The proposed method merges imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by using a privileged training procedure in which the teacher has access to full-state information. Using RL, we first obtain a teacher policy that is perception-aware; it is trained with full-state information to achieve minimum-time flight through cluttered environments. Afterwards, we apply imitation learning to distill this teacher into a vision-based student policy that perceives the scene only via a camera. By tightly coupling perception and control, our approach shows a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and in success rate. We validate closed-loop control performance in hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

author: Smith
title: Small, Fast, Effective: Pretrained Language Models for Specific Domains
abstract: Large pre-trained models have delivered substantial success across numerous natural language processing tasks. However, their use in specific domains incurs domain shift and poses difficulties for fine-tuning and for online serving under latency and capacity constraints. We propose a general approach to produce small, fast and effective pre-trained models tailored to specific domains. The approach adapts off-the-shelf general pre-trained models and applies task-agnostic knowledge distillation within target domains. Concretely, we introduce domain-specific vocabulary expansion during the adaptation stage and use corpus level occurrence probability to automatically determine the size of the incremental vocabulary. We then systematically evaluate a variety of strategies to compress the large pre-trained models for specific domains. Experiments are carried out in the biomedical and computer science domains. Results show that the proposed approach outperforms the BERT BASE model on domain-specific tasks while being 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. The code and pre-trained models are available at the project web page.

author: Nguyen
title: Knowledge Distillation for Small-footprint Highway Deep Models
abstract: Over the last few years, deep learning has driven substantial improvements in state-of-the-art speech recognition. However, neural network acoustic models are typically much larger than conventional Gaussian mixture acoustic models, which makes deployment on embedded devices difficult. In earlier work we examined a compact highway deep neural model for acoustic modelling; this architecture is a depth-gated feedforward neural network. We demonstrated that acoustic models based on this compact highway design can match the recognition accuracy of plain deep neural network (DNN) acoustic models while requiring far fewer parameters. In the present study, we advance this line by applying knowledge distillation, also known as teacher-student training, where the compact highway model is trained under supervision from a high-accuracy but cumbersome teacher model. We also study sequence training and adaptation within the teacher-student training paradigm. Experiments are conducted on the AMI meeting speech recognition corpus. With these techniques, we significantly improved the recognition accuracy of the compact highway acoustic model with less than 0.8 million parameters, narrowing the gap between this small-footprint model and a plain DNN with 30 million parameters.
